sections.title: Chapter 1 — cell injury
sections.description: Internal verified Chapter 1 source facts; retained for authoring, not an approved Memorize tab or shipping card collection.

cards.title: Four aspects of disease
cards.summary: Separate cause, development, structure and function.

facts.label: Etiology
facts.text: Identifies the cause: acquired/environmental, genetic/intrinsic or multifactorial.

review.reviewNotes: p8 names acquired/environmental, genetic/intrinsic and multifactorial causes.

facts.label: Pathogenesis
facts.text: The mechanism and sequence from the initial stimulus through cellular and tissue responses to disease expression.

review.reviewNotes: p10 defines mechanism and sequence from initial stimulus to disease expression.

facts.label: Morphology
facts.text: Structural alterations in cells and organs, including gross and microscopic changes.

review.reviewNotes: p12 includes gross and microscopic structural changes in cells/organs.

facts.label: Clinical significance
facts.text: Functional consequences of morphologic changes, expressed as symptoms and signs.

review.reviewNotes: p15 connects functional consequences with symptoms and signs.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: General, systemic and diagnostic subdivisions
cards.summary: Keep the object of study distinct.

facts.label: General versus systemic
facts.text: General pathology studies basic cellular and tissue reactions; systemic pathology describes specific diseases affecting organs or organ systems.

review.reviewNotes: pp19–20 distinguish basic cellular/tissue reactions from individual-organ disease.

facts.label: Tissue versus isolated cells
facts.text: Histopathology examines tissues; cytopathology examines isolated cells, including Pap smears and FNA.

review.reviewNotes: pp22–23 distinguish tissue examination from isolated cells and name Pap/FNA.

facts.label: Hematology
facts.text: Disorders of cellular and coagulable blood components, including blood smears, marrow and coagulation disorders.

review.reviewNotes: p25 names cellular/coagulable blood components, blood/marrow examples.

facts.label: Forensic pathology
facts.text: Application of pathology to legal purposes, including suspicious-death investigation and autopsy.

review.reviewNotes: p26 explicitly links legal use, suspicious death and autopsy.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Hypoxia and ischemia
cards.summary: Loss of blood supply affects oxygen and nutrients.

facts.label: Hypoxia
facts.text: Oxygen deficiency interferes with aerobic oxidative respiration.

review.reviewNotes: p14 links oxygen deficiency to aerobic oxidative respiration.

facts.label: Ischemia
facts.text: Loss of tissue blood supply reduces oxygen and nutrients; reduced glucose delivery is shown in the diagram.

review.reviewNotes: pp14–15 show blood-flow loss reducing oxygen plus nutrient/glucose supply.

facts.label: Other hypoxic settings
facts.text: Anemia, high altitude, respiratory failure and CO are shown as causes of reduced blood oxygenation.

review.reviewNotes: p15 diagram lists anemia/high altitude/respiratory failure/CO at reduced blood oxygenation branch; no saturation-specific claim added.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Injury targets and cell fate
cards.summary: Target, duration and severity shape the result.

facts.label: Response determinants
facts.text: Cellular responses depend on the type, duration and severity of injury.

review.reviewNotes: p19 states type, duration and severity as determinants.

facts.label: Reversibility
facts.text: Mild transient injury may be reversible; severe progressive injury leads to irreversible injury and death by necrosis or apoptosis.

review.reviewNotes: p3 branches mild/transient reversible versus severe/progressive irreversible, with both death forms.

facts.label: Membrane consequences
facts.text: Plasma membrane damage permits loss of contents; lysosomal damage permits enzymatic digestion of cellular components.

review.reviewNotes: p22 explicitly links plasma membrane to contents loss and lysosome to enzymatic digestion.

facts.label: Mitochondria
facts.text: ATP failure and increased ROS contribute to necrosis; leakage of pro-apoptotic mitochondrial proteins contributes to apoptosis.

review.reviewNotes: pp26–27 show ATP/ROS necrosis branch and pro-apoptotic release apoptosis branch.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Calcium amplifies injury
cards.summary: A rise in cytosolic calcium activates several damaging routes.

facts.label: Calcium sources
facts.text: Extracellular influx and release from intracellular stores increase cytosolic calcium during injury.

review.reviewNotes: p24 arrows show extracellular influx and intracellular mitochondrial/ER release.

facts.label: Membrane injury
facts.text: Calcium activates phospholipases and proteases, reducing phospholipids and disrupting membrane/cytoskeletal proteins.

review.reviewNotes: p24 maps phospholipase to lower phospholipid and protease to membrane/cytoskeletal disruption.

facts.label: Nuclear and energy effects
facts.text: Endonucleases cause nuclear damage; ATPase activation contributes to ATP depletion.

review.reviewNotes: p24 maps endonuclease to nuclear damage and ATPase to lower ATP.

facts.label: Mitochondrial effect
facts.text: Increased calcium promotes mitochondrial permeability transition and ATP reduction.

review.reviewNotes: p24 separate mitochondrial permeability-transition arrow ends at lower ATP.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Consequences of ATP depletion
cards.summary: Follow the separate ionic, metabolic and synthetic branches.

facts.label: ATP production
facts.text: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and anaerobic glycolysis are the two supplied ATP-generation pathways.

review.reviewNotes: p25 names oxidative phosphorylation and anaerobic glycolysis as ATP-generation routes.

facts.label: Pump failure
facts.text: Reduced Na+ pump activity leads to Na+, water and Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux, with cellular/ER swelling, blebs and microvillus loss.

review.reviewNotes: p28 visual diagram shows Na/water/Ca influx, K loss and swelling/blebs/microvillus branch.

facts.label: Glycolysis
facts.text: Increased anaerobic glycolysis reduces glycogen and pH; low pH is connected to nuclear-chromatin clumping.

review.reviewNotes: p28 shows increased glycolysis, glycogen decrease, pH decrease and chromatin clumping.

facts.label: Protein synthesis
facts.text: Ribosome detachment reduces protein synthesis and is connected to lipid deposition.

review.reviewNotes: p28 shows ribosome detachment, lower synthesis and lipid deposition.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: ROS injury and removal
cards.summary: Keep targets and protective conversions separate.

facts.label: Free-radical definition
facts.text: An unstable chemical species with a single unpaired electron in the outer orbital.

review.reviewNotes: p29 outer-orbital unpaired-electron definition clear; no H2O2 free-radical classification included.

facts.label: Targets
facts.text: Lipid peroxidation damages membranes; protein modification causes breakdown/misfolding; DNA damage can produce mutation.

review.reviewNotes: p32 maps lipid/protein/DNA injury to membrane damage, breakdown/misfolding and mutation.

facts.label: Enzymatic removal
facts.text: SOD converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; catalase and glutathione peroxidase remove hydrogen peroxide.

review.reviewNotes: pp30/32 show SOD superoxide-to-peroxide, catalase/peroxidase peroxide removal.

facts.label: Antioxidants
facts.text: Endogenous or exogenous antioxidants can block free-radical formation or scavenge radicals; examples include vitamins E, A, C and beta-carotene.

review.reviewNotes: p33 states block formation/scavenge and vitamins E/A/C/beta-carotene.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Direct injury and metabolic activation
cards.summary: Two chemical-injury routes.

facts.label: Direct binding
facts.text: Mercury binds sulfhydryl groups of membrane proteins, inhibiting ATPase-dependent transport and increasing permeability.

review.reviewNotes: p34 explicitly gives mercury-sulfhydryl binding and ATPase transport/permeability effects.

facts.label: Activation
facts.text: P450 oxidases in smooth ER convert some initially inactive chemicals into reactive toxic metabolites; CCl4 and acetaminophen are supplied examples.

review.reviewNotes: p35 gives P450 in SER and CCl4/acetaminophen examples; no treatment advice added.

facts.label: CCl4 route
facts.text: CCl4 is converted to CCl3 radical in the liver, initiating lipid peroxidation.

review.reviewNotes: p36 shows CCl4 to CCl3 radical with lipid peroxidation.

facts.label: Fatty-liver branch
facts.text: RER injury causes polysome detachment and reduced apoprotein synthesis, leading to fatty liver.

review.reviewNotes: p36 links RER injury/polysome detachment to reduced apoprotein and fatty liver.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Size, number and cell type
cards.summary: The defining change separates the adaptive responses.

facts.label: Atrophy
facts.text: Loss of cell substance reduces cell size and function; affected cells remain alive.

review.reviewNotes: p8 gives substance loss, reduced size/function and surviving cells.

facts.label: Hypertrophy
facts.text: Existing cells enlarge; no new cells are produced by this response. It is prominent in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

review.reviewNotes: p18 says no new cells, bigger cells; cardiac/skeletal muscle named.

facts.label: Hyperplasia
facts.text: Increased cell number enlarges an organ; it requires cells capable of division.

review.reviewNotes: p24 defines increased number and division-capable tissue.

facts.label: Metaplasia
facts.text: One adult cell type replaces another through reprogramming of stem cells or undifferentiated mesenchymal cells.

review.reviewNotes: p29 gives stem-cell/undifferentiated-mesenchymal reprogramming rather than conversion of a fixed mature cell.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Atrophy triggers and protein turnover
cards.summary: Different causes share a basic loss of structural material.

facts.label: Triggers
facts.text: Decreased workload, denervation, diminished blood supply and inadequate nutrition are pathological causes; thymic involution, aging and menopausal hormone loss are supplied physiological examples.

review.reviewNotes: p9 explicitly separates supplied physiological and pathological causes, including menopause.

facts.label: Protein balance
facts.text: Decreased synthesis, increased catabolism or both reduce structural components. Fundamental cellular changes are identical in physiological and pathological atrophy.

review.reviewNotes: p12 states decreased synthesis/increased catabolism and shared fundamental changes.

facts.label: Lysosomal pathway
facts.text: Lysosomes degrade endocytosed proteins and subcellular organelles; organelle breakdown produces autophagic vacuoles.

review.reviewNotes: p13 distinguishes endocytosed proteins/subcellular organelles and autophagic vacuoles.

facts.label: Proteasome pathway
facts.text: Ubiquitin tags damaged proteins for non-lysosomal proteasomal degradation; the diagram shows ubiquitin recycling.

review.reviewNotes: pp15–16 give ubiquitin tagging, nonlysosomal proteasome degradation and recycling in diagram.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Growth responses and their limits
cards.summary: Stimulus-dependent enlargement can reverse.

facts.label: Gravid uterus
facts.text: Estrogen stimulates both smooth-muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

review.reviewNotes: pp19/25 show estrogen with smooth-muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia in pregnancy.

facts.label: Cardiac triggers
facts.text: Mechanical stretch and trophic alpha-adrenergic receptor activation are supplied triggers of cardiac hypertrophy.

review.reviewNotes: p21 labels stretch and alpha-adrenergic trophic trigger.

facts.label: Hyperplasia settings
facts.text: Physiological hyperplasia may be hormonal or compensatory; liver resection and wound healing are supplied compensatory examples.

review.reviewNotes: p26 names hormonal/compensatory, liver resection and wound healing.

facts.label: Removal and risk
facts.text: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia can reverse after stimulus removal; pathological hyperplasia may provide a setting for later cancerous proliferation.

review.reviewNotes: p27 explicitly states both responses reverse and pathological hyperplasia may precede cancerous growth.

facts.label: Limits
facts.text: Adaptive hypertrophy may change phenotype and contractile-protein type; degenerative change can eventually lead to organ failure.

review.reviewNotes: p22 describes phenotype/contractile-protein change and later degeneration/failure; disputed p20 causal direction excluded.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Metaplasia examples
cards.summary: Replacement depends on tissue and persistent stimulus.

facts.label: Bronchial example
facts.text: Cigarette smoke is paired with replacement of bronchial ciliated columnar epithelium by squamous epithelium.

review.reviewNotes: p30 pairs smoke with ciliated columnar-to-squamous bronchial epithelium.

facts.label: Esophageal example
facts.text: Gastric acid is paired with replacement of esophageal squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium, termed Barrett metaplasia.

review.reviewNotes: pp30–31 pair acid reflux with squamous-to-columnar Barrett change.

facts.label: Mesenchymal example
facts.text: Chronic trauma is paired with replacement of fibrocollagenous tissue by bone tissue.

review.reviewNotes: p30 pairs chronic trauma with fibrocollagenous tissue-to-bone.

facts.label: Persistent stimulus
facts.text: Persistent influences that induce metaplasia may also induce cancer transformation in the metaplastic epithelium.

review.reviewNotes: p29 qualifies cancer transformation by persistent inducing influences, not inevitability.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Autophagy, heterophagy and residual material
cards.summary: Distinguish internal organelles from external material.

facts.label: Secondary lysosome
facts.text: Fusion of a primary lysosome with a material-containing digestive vacuole produces a secondary lysosome/phagolysosome.

review.reviewNotes: p3 defines fusion yielding secondary/phagolysosome.

facts.label: Autophagy
facts.text: Intracellular organelles are sequestered in an autophagic vacuole that fuses with a primary lysosome; especially seen in atrophy and aging.

review.reviewNotes: p7 explicitly gives own-organelle sequestration and primary lysosome fusion in aging/atrophy.

facts.label: Heterophagy
facts.text: Inflammatory cells engulf external material; neutrophils degrade bacteria and macrophages catabolize necrotic cells.

review.reviewNotes: p8 gives inflammatory cells, neutrophil bacteria and macrophage necrotic-cell examples.

facts.label: Uptake size
facts.text: Pinocytosis engulfs small soluble material; phagocytosis engulfs large material.

review.reviewNotes: p8 explicitly separates small soluble uptake from large material uptake.

facts.label: Residual material
facts.text: Undigested debris may persist as residual bodies or be extruded. Indigestible carbon can remain in macrophage phagolysosomes for decades.

review.reviewNotes: p9 gives retained/extruded residual bodies and carbon persisting decades.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Other subcellular responses
cards.summary: Enzyme induction, organelle adaptation and protein repair.

facts.label: Smooth ER
facts.text: SER/P450 induction increases compound solubility and facilitates excretion; the phenobarbital/alcohol example describes possible subtherapeutic drug levels.

review.reviewNotes: p10 states solubility/excretion effect and phenobarbital/alcohol subtherapeutic-level example; reference description only.

facts.label: Mitochondria
facts.text: Mitochondrial number increases in hypertrophy and decreases in atrophy; alcoholic liver disease illustrates large abnormally shaped megamitochondria.

review.reviewNotes: p11 gives number changes and large abnormal alcoholic-liver megamitochondria.

facts.label: Cytoskeleton
facts.text: Microtubules are essential for leukocyte migration and phagocytosis; immotile respiratory cilia impair bacterial clearance.

review.reviewNotes: p12 gives leukocyte migration/phagocytosis and immotile-cilia clearance; gout-specific macrophage claim excluded.

facts.label: Chaperones
facts.text: Heat shock proteins participate in protein folding, disaggregation and transport.

review.reviewNotes: p13 directly names folding/disaggregation/transport.

facts.label: Failed protein repair
facts.text: Denatured proteins may be refolded; failure of repair directs proteins to ubiquitin-proteasome degradation.

review.reviewNotes: pp14–15 connect refolding attempt to ubiquitin/proteasome on failed repair; stress-only absolute excluded.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Reversible injury
cards.summary: Functional change may precede visible morphology.

facts.label: Detection timing
facts.text: The graph places functional change before morphologic change, with ultrastructure detected before light-microscopic and gross changes.

review.reviewNotes: p2 graph places functional decline before ultrastructural, light and gross detection; not a numerical time claim.

facts.label: ER and nucleus
facts.text: ER dilation with ribosome loss and clumping of nuclear chromatin are described in reversible injury.

review.reviewNotes: p10 explicitly names ER dilation/ribosome loss and chromatin clumping.

facts.label: Hydropic change
facts.text: Loss of ionic/fluid homeostasis produces cellular swelling with clear vacuoles from distended and pinched-off ER segments.

review.reviewNotes: p12 directly gives ionic/fluid-homeostasis loss and distended pinched-off ER vacuoles.

facts.label: Fatty change
facts.text: Lipid vacuoles occur in cells handling fat metabolism, with liver and heart supplied examples.

review.reviewNotes: p13 names fat-metabolizing cells, liver and heart.

facts.label: Gross change
facts.text: Increased organ weight and pallor are the supplied gross reversible changes.

review.reviewNotes: p14 explicitly gives increased weight/pallor.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Irreversibility and necrotic clearance
cards.summary: Membrane failure and sustained mitochondrial dysfunction mark the limit.

facts.label: Point of no return
facts.text: Inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction and severe membrane damage characterize irreversibility.

review.reviewNotes: p20 names inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction and severe membrane damage.

facts.label: Digestion source
facts.text: Autolysis uses the cell’s own enzymes; heterolysis uses lysosomal enzymes from other cells.

review.reviewNotes: p18 gives own enzymes versus lysosomes from other cells.

facts.label: Clearance
facts.text: Extracellular enzymatic digestion and leukocyte phagocytosis remove most necrotic material; retained debris may undergo dystrophic calcification.

review.reviewNotes: p19 names extracellular digestion/leukocyte phagocytosis and retained-debris dystrophic calcium.

facts.label: Necrosis
facts.text: Morphologic changes follow cell death in living tissue and require hours to develop.

review.reviewNotes: p24 defines morphology after death in living tissue; p19 explicitly supplies hours-to-develop qualifier, now additionally cited.

facts.label: Cytoplasm
facts.text: Eosin binding to denatured proteins and RNA loss increase eosinophilia; glycogen loss makes cytoplasm glassy and organelle degeneration makes it vacuolated.

review.reviewNotes: p27 directly gives eosin binding/RNA loss, glycogen/glassy and organelle/vacuolated changes.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Necrotic nuclear changes
cards.summary: Definitions, without imposing a mandatory sequence.

facts.label: Pyknosis
facts.text: Nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia.

review.reviewNotes: p28 defines shrinkage/increased basophilia.

facts.label: Karyorrhexis
facts.text: Fragmentation of a pyknotic nucleus by nucleases.

review.reviewNotes: p28 defines pyknotic nucleus fragmentation by nucleases.

facts.label: Karyolysis
facts.text: Loss of chromatin basophilia secondary to DNase activity.

review.reviewNotes: p28 defines basophilia loss with DNase activity.

facts.label: Time window
facts.text: The source states complete nuclear disappearance one to two days after cell death.

review.reviewNotes: p28 gives 1–2 days to complete nuclear disappearance; preserved as source-qualified, no universal sequence invented.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Patterns of necrosis
cards.summary: Architecture, substrate and setting discriminate the patterns.

facts.label: Coagulative
facts.text: Protein denaturation predominates and basic tissue outlines persist for days; hypoxia/ischemia in most organs is the setting, except brain.

review.reviewNotes: p3 preserves outlines for days and names denaturation dominance, most ischemic organs except brain.

facts.label: Liquefactive
facts.text: Enzymatic digestion predominates and architecture is destroyed; ischemic brain and bacterial/fungal infections are supplied settings.

review.reviewNotes: p11 gives digestion dominance, lost architecture, brain ischemia and bacterial/fungal settings.

facts.label: Caseous
facts.text: Tuberculous infection is associated with cheesy white foci and amorphous granular debris, with architecture obliterated.

review.reviewNotes: p14 gives TB, cheesy white foci and granular debris with lost architecture.

facts.label: Fat
facts.text: Pancreatic enzyme release causes focal fat destruction; saponification appears chalky white and calcified cell shadows appear microscopically.

review.reviewNotes: p17 gives pancreatic enzymes, focal fat destruction, saponification and calcified cell shadows.

facts.label: Gangrene
facts.text: Dry gangrene is ischemic coagulative necrosis; infection with a liquefactive component produces wet gangrene.

review.reviewNotes: p19 gives dry ischemic coagulation and infected wet liquefactive component.

facts.label: Fibrinoid
facts.text: Small-vessel injury involves fibrin/plasma-protein accumulation and intensely red-staining necrotic areas.

review.reviewNotes: p21 visual figure labels fibrin/plasma proteins and intensely red necrotic small-vessel injury.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Apoptotic pathways
cards.summary: Initiation, regulation, execution and removal.

facts.label: Caspase roles
facts.text: Initiators establish commitment to apoptosis; effectors produce structural degradation.

review.reviewNotes: p7 clear functional distinction retained; absolute distribution removed from fact text and documented as source restriction.

facts.label: Intrinsic pathway
facts.text: Growth-factor withdrawal, DNA damage and protein misfolding converge on mitochondrial pro-apoptotic release, initiator and executioner caspases.

review.reviewNotes: p15 shows three intrinsic triggers -> mitochondrial release -> initiator/executioner route, avoiding p10 bypass ambiguity.

facts.label: Extrinsic pathway
facts.text: Fas/TNF death-receptor interactions act through adaptor proteins and initiator caspases.

review.reviewNotes: p15 shows Fas/TNF -> adapters -> initiators.

facts.label: BCL-2 balance
facts.text: BCL-2/BCL-XL support survival by preventing cytochrome c leakage; sensor-driven BCL-2 antagonism and Bax/Bak activation favor release.

review.reviewNotes: p16 shows survival proteins preventing leakage and sensors/Bax/Bak favoring release; no direct Apaf binding scored.

facts.label: Execution and removal
facts.text: Proteases and endonucleases break down cytoskeletal/nuclear structures; apoptotic bodies express ligands for phagocytic binding and uptake.

review.reviewNotes: p12 names proteases/endonucleases, structural breakdown and new ligands for phagocyte recognition.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Necrosis and apoptosis
cards.summary: Compare size, membrane, contents and tissue reaction.

facts.label: Size
facts.text: Necrosis enlarges cells by swelling; apoptosis reduces cell size.

review.reviewNotes: p21 contrasts swelling/increase with shrinkage.

facts.label: Membrane and contents
facts.text: Necrosis disrupts membranes with digestion and possible leakage; apoptosis preserves an altered intact membrane and packages contents in bodies.

review.reviewNotes: p21 contrasts disrupted/digested/leaking with intact-altered membrane/intact bodies.

facts.label: Inflammation
facts.text: Necrosis frequently has adjacent inflammation; apoptotic cells are described without surrounding inflammatory cells.

review.reviewNotes: pp17/21 give no adjacent apoptosis inflammation versus frequent necrosis inflammation.

facts.label: Role
facts.text: Necrosis is pathological in the supplied comparison; apoptosis often eliminates unwanted cells physiologically and may also follow injury.

review.reviewNotes: p21 contrasts pathological necrosis and often physiological/sometimes injury-related apoptosis.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Steatosis mechanisms
cards.summary: Input, oxidation and export can each affect fat accumulation.

facts.label: Definition
facts.text: Reversible triglyceride accumulation within parenchymal cells, most commonly liver; heart, skeletal muscle and kidney may also be affected.

review.reviewNotes: p7 gives TG/parenchymal/reversible and liver emphasis with other named organs; no exclusive distribution.

facts.label: Input and oxidation
facts.text: Diabetes/starvation increase FFA supply; hypoxia reduces fatty-acid oxidation in the supplied mechanism diagram.

review.reviewNotes: p11 arrows show diabetes/starvation supply increase versus hypoxia oxidation decrease.

facts.label: Export
facts.text: Protein malnutrition reduces apoprotein availability, impairing triglyceride export via lipoproteins.

review.reviewNotes: pp8/11 give reduced apoprotein and impaired export from malnutrition.

facts.label: Morphology
facts.text: Early small perinuclear fat vacuoles progress with an enlarged yellow, greasy and soft organ.

review.reviewNotes: p12 supplies early perinuclear vacuoles and progressive gross enlargement/yellow/greasy/soft.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Protein and lipid inclusions
cards.summary: Use compartment and substance to distinguish inclusions.

facts.label: Foam cells
facts.text: Cholesterol and cholesterol esters accumulate in macrophages; smooth-muscle cells and macrophages in plaques contain lipid vacuoles that contribute yellow color.

review.reviewNotes: p15 gives cholesterol/esters in foam cells and plaque smooth muscle/macrophages/yellow lipid.

facts.label: Xanthomas
facts.text: Foamy cholesterol-containing macrophages form masses in skin subepithelial connective tissue or tendons.

review.reviewNotes: p16 gives skin subepithelial connective tissue/tendon foamy macrophages.

facts.label: Russell bodies
facts.text: Newly synthesized immunoglobulins accumulate in the RER of plasma cells.

review.reviewNotes: p17 gives newly synthesized Ig in plasma-cell RER.

facts.label: Mallory bodies
facts.text: Eosinophilic prekeratin-filament inclusions in liver cells are supplied in alcoholic liver disease.

review.reviewNotes: p18 gives alcoholic-liver prekeratin eosinophilic inclusions.

facts.label: Tangles
facts.text: The Alzheimer-disease brain example contains aggregated microtubule-associated proteins and neurofilaments.

review.reviewNotes: p18 gives Alzheimer aggregated microtubule-associated proteins/neurofilaments; outside tau naming absent.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Pigment distinctions
cards.summary: Origin and material distinguish similarly colored deposits.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.text: The supplied most common exogenous pigment; aggregates in lung and hilar nodes are termed anthracosis.

review.reviewNotes: p22 gives most common exogenous carbon and lung/hilar aggregates.

facts.label: Lipofuscin
facts.text: Brownish-yellow wear-and-tear lipid-protein material from membrane peroxidation, accumulating with age/atrophy; gross pigment is brown atrophy.

review.reviewNotes: pp25–26 give lipid-protein peroxidation residue, age/atrophy and gross brown atrophy.

facts.label: Melanin
facts.text: Brown-black pigment produced by melanocytes and also accumulated by basal keratinocytes or dermal macrophages.

review.reviewNotes: p27 distinguishes melanocyte production from keratinocyte/macrophage accumulation.

facts.label: Hemosiderin
facts.text: Golden-yellow/brown hemoglobin-derived pigment composed of large ferritin aggregates, associated with excess iron and detected by Prussian blue.

review.reviewNotes: p29 gives Hb-derived ferritin aggregates, golden/yellow/brown, excess iron and Prussian blue.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.

cards.title: Dystrophic and metastatic calcification
cards.summary: Tissue status and serum calcium are the central comparison.

facts.label: Dystrophic
facts.text: Calcium deposits in dead/dying tissue with normal serum calcium; deposits are fine white granules grossly and basophilic microscopically.

review.reviewNotes: p32 gives dead/dying tissue, normal calcium, fine white granules and basophilia.

facts.label: Valve consequence
facts.text: Dystrophic calcification of the aortic valve is an important supplied cause of aortic stenosis in the elderly.

review.reviewNotes: p33 explicitly names aortic-valve calcification/stenosis in elderly; retained reference fact without forcing weak question.

facts.label: Metastatic
facts.text: Calcium deposition in normal tissue in the presence of hypercalcemia.

review.reviewNotes: p34 gives normal tissue plus hypercalcemia; unqualified renal failure generalization excluded.

facts.label: Sites and severity
facts.text: Metastatic deposition mainly affects interstitium of blood vessels, kidneys, lungs and gastric mucosa; dysfunction generally requires severe disease, with nephrocalcinosis supplied as an example.

review.reviewNotes: p35 lists principal sites without exclusivity and severe-function qualifier/nephrocalcinosis.
Every fact checked against independently inspected original images; title and summary match the facts. Internal authoring reference only; no approved product-tab claim.
All 104 facts in 24 cards checked against original source images. Not approved as a shipping Memorize tab/card collection. Antigravity and Claude pending.
